description: cypher_space_01 is a crew of builders from Beni Mellal who turn curiosity into code and wild ideas into launches. This Space Apps, we’re taking on astronaut health: software that keeps crews safe on Mars when Mission Control is 20 minutes away, and brings the same care to remote places on Earth. Our mission is clear and our crew is ready. Ground control, stand by: Beni Mellal is going to space.
summary: Astro Vital is a crew health monitoring prototype that shows when a health assessment has enough evidence and when it doesn't. A crew member opens a dashboard, moves a replay clock, and gets one clear assessment; Why? opens the exact rule, the readings with IDs and timestamps, the baselines and the missing inputs behind it. Today it demonstrates two cases: a real NASA RadLab detector replay where one detector goes stale while the other keeps reporting, and a synthetic sleep + vigilance check where missing reaction data keeps the assessment pending until a 310 ms sample (24% above the 250 ms baseline) plus two short nights trigger Sleep and vigilance change.
details:
What it is :

Astro Vital is a prototype that helps an astronaut judge whether the evidence behind a health assessment is good enough to act on. Most dashboards show a score. Astro Vital instead shows the assessment, the readings and baselines behind it, what data is missing or stale, and the next action. It treats missing, stale and incomparable data as real outcomes and refuses to invent a number when an input is absent.

The two demos :

The first uses real NASA RadLab detector readings from the ISS Columbus module (180 readings from two detectors, pinned by checksum). At 23:17:26 one detector has been silent for 301 seconds, so the rule marks it stale and opens one incident. At 23:30 it reports again and the incident resolves. The tool says the cause of the gap is unknown, and it clarifies that these are cabin readings, not a personal radiation dose. The second demo uses synthetic crew data. At 09:00 the reaction-time result is missing, so the assessment stays “insufficient data” and names the missing input. At 09:01 a seeded 310 ms reaction (24% slower than the 250 ms baseline), combined with two short nights of sleep, produces a “watch” result. Rewinding the clock removes anything that happened later, so nothing from the future leaks in.

How it works :

A pure, deterministic rule engine, SOURCE_FRESHNESS and SLEEP_VIGILANCE, evaluates only the observations visible at a chosen UTC clock. The front end never recomputes anything and just displays what the engine returns, with a “Why?” drawer showing the exact readings, baselines, IDs and provenance. Data is labelled in three classes that are never mixed: real historical, synthetic, and live-measured (a reaction check the user actually performs in the browser, which is deliberately marked as not comparable with the synthetic baseline). The API validates everything before saving, and retried submissions are handled safely (201 for the first insert, 200 for an identical retry, 409 for a changed payload).

Tools used :

The front end is React 19 with TypeScript and Vite. The back end is FastAPI with SQLite, and everything runs as one local process on loopback with bundled fonts and artwork and no CDN. Testing uses pytest (187 tests), Vitest and Node tests (91 and 41), plus an end-to-end runtime gate. The design uses an “orbital observatory” look with Fira Sans, and the anatomy artwork is AI-generated.
projectRefs: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
